Functional Dependencies and Normalization

Chapters 14 & 15 of Elmasri & Navathe (7th ed.). Exercises 14.2–14.12, 14.19–14.34, 15.1–15.12, 15.21, 15.24. Each topic below opens with its theory; the exercise topics give every assigned question with a full solution behind the Solution button. Questions marked must-do match past end-sem and quiz questions.

The story of this topic

A correct mapping can still give tables with redundancy, and redundancy causes update anomalies. Functional dependencies state which attributes determine which; the normal forms are tests built on them; the decomposition algorithms fix a bad schema without losing information. Almost every question here runs on the attribute closure. Compute it step by step and the keys, normal-form checks and lossless-join test follow from it.

How the exercises are solved

Every assigned exercise, in textbook order. Each solution is written the way the Moodle keys are: assumptions with reasons, every step shown, and the final answer in an Answer box. Start with the exercises tagged ★ Must-do; they match past end-sem and quiz questions.

What is inside

    1  How to read this part

    Theory recap

    Normalization questions carry many marks and are graded step by step. This part follows the book (Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 14 and 15) and the style of the course’s Moodle keys (N-I key and rubric, GA4 detailed solutions and rubric). One small schema is the running example for every algorithm, so you can see the whole pipeline on one input:

    R(A,B,C,D,E,F),F={ AB→C,  C→BDE,  D→E,  ABD→F }.R(A,B,C,D,E,F),\qquad F=\{\ AB \rightarrow C,\ \ C \rightarrow BDE,\ \ D \rightarrow E,\ \ ABD \rightarrow F\ \}.R(A,B,C,D,E,F),F={ AB→C,  C→BDE,  D→E,  ABD→F }.
    How normalization answers are graded (N-I and GA4 rubrics)
    • Closures with steps. Write each closure as a chain, naming the FD used at each step (e.g. C→C→FGCFG→F→AACFGC\xrightarrow{C\to FG}CFG\xrightarrow{F\to A}ACFGCC→FG​CFGF→A​ACFG). A closure stated without steps gets half marks.
    • Keys justified. Say why each key is a key (K+=RK^+=RK+=R) and why it is minimal (no proper subset is a superkey). “CCC is on no right side, so CCC is in every key” is the expected argument. Giving a superkey such as CKLCKLCKL as a key scores 0 for that line.
    • Prime and non-prime attributes listed explicitly.
    • Each violation with its reason: name the FD, say which part of the definition fails (“C⊂CKC\subset CKC⊂CK, and F,GF,GF,G are non-prime, so a partial dependency: 2NF fails”). A violation named without a reason gets half marks.
    • Every decomposition step: the violating FD X→YX\to YX→Y used, the two pieces XYXYXY and Ri−(Y−X)R_i-(Y-X)Ri​−(Y−X), and the FDs that hold in each piece including derived ones (projected FDs).
    • Final relations each with their key, and a statement that each is in the target normal form.
    • Lossless join proved: “the common attributes are a key of one side” for each split, or a chase table. Dependency preservation: discuss it for 3NF; for BCNF it is not required, but saying what is lost is good.
    • Error carried forward: a mistake is penalised once; later parts are graded against your own earlier result, so always show the method even if you doubt an earlier answer.
    • Not unique: decompositions and minimal covers are checked against the definition, not against one model answer. A correct final answer without working earns only the final-answer mark.
    • Assumptions earn marks only when stated and justified (e.g. “attributes are atomic”, “the given FDs are the complete set; keys are judged by F+F^+F+, not by sample data”).

    2  Informal design guidelines · Ch. 14.1

    Theory recap

    The book gives four informal measures of the quality of a relation schema. They are not independent; the formal theory (FDs and normal forms) later makes guidelines 2 and 4 precise.

    Guideline 1: clear semantics

    Guideline 1

    Design each relation so that its meaning is easy to explain. Do not combine attributes of several entity types and relationship types into one relation. A relation that matches one entity type or one relationship type (as a correct ER-to-relational mapping produces) is easy to explain.

    Example of a violation: EMP_DEPT(Ename, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn) mixes employee facts with department facts; EMP_PROJ(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Ename, Pname, Plocation) mixes employee, project and WORKS_ON facts. Neither is logically wrong (both are fine as views), but as base relations they cause the problems below.

    Guideline 2: no redundancy, hence no update anomalies

    Storing a join as a base relation repeats data. In EMP_DEPT the triple (Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn) is repeated for every employee of the department:

    EnameSsnDnumberDnameDmgr_ssn
    Smith1234567895Research333445555
    Wong3334455555Research333445555
    Narayan6668844445Research333445555
    Zelaya9998877774Administration987654321
    Borg8886655551Headquarters888665555

    This redundancy causes three kinds of update anomalies:

    Definition: Insertion, deletion and modification anomalies
    • Insertion anomaly. (a) Inserting a new employee forces you to type the department’s values again, consistently with every other tuple of that department (or NULLs). (b) A new department with no employees cannot be inserted without NULLs in the employee attributes, and Ssn is the primary key, so NULL is forbidden (entity integrity).
    • Deletion anomaly. Deleting the last employee of a department (e.g. Borg, the only employee of dept. 1) also deletes the only record of that department.
    • Modification anomaly. Changing a department fact (the manager of dept. 5) must be done in every tuple of that department; missing one leaves the database inconsistent (two managers for dept. 5).

    In EMP_PROJ the same happens with projects: a project with no employees cannot be inserted, deleting the last WORKS_ON tuple of a project loses the project, and renaming a project means updating many tuples.

    Guideline 2

    Design base relations so that no insertion, deletion or modification anomalies occur. If some are allowed (for performance, e.g. a materialized view), note them clearly and make sure update programs handle them (e.g. with triggers). Storing the join of normalized relations as a base relation is called denormalization.

    Guideline 3: avoid frequent NULLs

    A “fat” relation whose attributes do not apply to many tuples has many NULLs. NULLs waste space, make the meaning unclear, and complicate joins (inner vs. outer joins give different results) and aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG skip NULLs; comparisons give unknown). A NULL can also mean three different things: not applicable, unknown, or exists but not recorded, and a single NULL cannot say which.

    Guideline 3

    Avoid attributes in a base relation whose values may frequently be NULL; if NULLs are unavoidable they should apply to exceptional tuples only. Example: if only 15% of employees have an office, store EMP_OFFICES(Essn, Office_number) separately instead of a mostly-NULL column in EMPLOYEE.

    Guideline 4: no spurious tuples

    Split EMP_PROJ into EMP_LOCS(Ename, Plocation) and EMP_PROJ1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname, Plocation). The only common attribute is Plocation, which is neither a key nor a foreign key of either relation. Joining them back pairs every project at a location with every employee who works anywhere at that location, e.g. (123456789, 1, 32.5, ProductX, Bellaire, English) although English’s Ssn is 453453453. Such tuples, present in the join but not in the original, are spurious tuples.

    Guideline 4

    Design relations so that they are joined with equality conditions on (primary key, foreign key) pairs, so that no spurious tuples are generated. Avoid relations whose matching attributes are not (FK, PK) combinations. The formal version is the lossless (nonadditive) join property (Section 6.3).

    3  Functional dependencies · Ch. 14.2

    Theory recap
    Definition: Functional dependency

    For X,Y⊆RX,Y\subseteq RX,Y⊆R, the FD X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y is a constraint on every legal state rrr of RRR: for any two tuples t1,t2∈rt_1,t_2\in rt1​,t2​∈r,  t1[X]=t2[X] ⟹ t1[Y]=t2[Y]t_1[X]=t_2[X]\ \Longrightarrow\ t_1[Y]=t_2[Y]t1​[X]=t2​[X] ⟹ t1​[Y]=t2​[Y]. “XXX functionally determines YYY”; XXX is the left-hand side (LHS), YYY the right-hand side (RHS). The FD is trivial if Y⊆XY\subseteq XY⊆X (it holds in every state); otherwise non-trivial.

    • If KKK is a candidate key, no two tuples agree on KKK, so K→YK \rightarrow YK→Y for every Y⊆RY\subseteq RY⊆R.
    • X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y says nothing about Y→XY \rightarrow XY→X; and XY→AXY \rightarrow AXY→A does not imply X→AX \rightarrow AX→A (you cannot split a left side).
    • Sources of FDs: the meaning of the attributes, i.e. the designer’s knowledge of the application (business rules, requirements, laws such as “one driving licence number per state”). FDs may stop holding when the world changes (Zip_code →\to→ Area_code once did).

    An FD is a property of the schema, not of a state

    What a relation instance can and cannot show

    An FD must hold in every legal state, and a given state is only one of them. Therefore:

    • a state can disprove an FD: two tuples that agree on XXX but differ on YYY show X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y does not hold;
    • a state can never prove an FD: if no pair violates it, the FD may hold, nothing more.

    Keys are likewise properties of the schema; never read them from sample data.

    Figure 14.8: what may hold, what cannot
    AAABBBCCCDDD
    t1t_1t1​a1b1c1d1
    t2t_2t2​a1b2c2d2
    t3t_3t3​a2b2c2d3
    t4t_4t4​a3b3c4d3

    Cannot hold: A→BA \rightarrow BA→B (t1,t2t_1,t_2t1​,t2​ agree on AAA, differ on BBB); B→AB \rightarrow AB→A (t2,t3t_2,t_3t2​,t3​); D→CD \rightarrow CD→C (t3,t4t_3,t_4t3​,t4​).

    May hold (not violated here): B→CB \rightarrow CB→C, C→BC \rightarrow BC→B, AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C, AB→DAB \rightarrow DAB→D, CD→BCD \rightarrow BCD→B. Only the semantics can decide whether they hold.

    4  Keys and normal forms · Ch. 14.3–14.7

    Theory recap

    Keys, prime attributes, and the three kinds of dependency

    Definition: Superkey, key, prime attribute

    A superkey is a set S⊆RS\subseteq RS⊆R with no two legal tuples agreeing on SSS; equivalently S+=RS^+=RS+=R. A (candidate) key is a minimal superkey: removing any attribute makes it not a superkey. One candidate key is chosen as primary key. An attribute is prime if it belongs to some candidate key, non-prime otherwise.

    Definition: Full, partial and transitive dependency
    • X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y is a full dependency if for every A∈XA\in XA∈X, (X−{A})↛Y(X-\{A\})\not\to Y(X−{A})→Y.
    • It is a partial dependency if some A∈XA\in XA∈X can be removed and (X−{A})→Y(X-\{A\})\to Y(X−{A})→Y still holds. In normalization: a non-prime attribute determined by a proper subset of a key.
    • X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y is transitive if there is a set ZZZ that is neither a candidate key nor a subset of any key, with X→ZX \rightarrow ZX→Z and Z→YZ \rightarrow YZ→Y. In normalization: key →\to→ non-key set →\to→ non-prime attribute.

    Example (EMP_PROJ): {Ssn,Pnumber}→Hours\{\textsf{Ssn},\textsf{Pnumber}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Hours}{Ssn,Pnumber}→Hours is full; {Ssn,Pnumber}→Ename\{\textsf{Ssn},\textsf{Pnumber}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Ename}{Ssn,Pnumber}→Ename is partial because Ssn→Ename\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \textsf{Ename}Ssn→Ename. (EMP_DEPT): Ssn→Dmgr_ssn\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \textsf{Dmgr\_ssn}Ssn→Dmgr_ssn is transitive via Dnumber\textsf{Dnumber}Dnumber.

    First normal form

    Definition: 1NF

    Every attribute’s domain contains only atomic (indivisible) values and every attribute value in a tuple is a single value from its domain. 1NF forbids multivalued attributes, composite attributes and nested relations (“relations within relations”). It is now part of the definition of a flat relation.

    Example:
    DEPARTMENT(Dname, Dnumber, Dmgr_ssn, Dlocations) with Dlocations ={=\{={Bellaire, Sugarland, Houston}\}} for dept. 5 is not in 1NF. Three ways to fix it:

    TechniqueResultVerdict
    1. Move the attribute to a new relationDEPARTMENT(Dname, Dnumber, Dmgr_ssn) and DEPT_LOCATIONS(Dnumber, Dlocation)Best: no redundancy, no limit on the number of values.
    2. Expand the key (one tuple per value)DEPARTMENT(Dname, Dnumber, Dmgr_ssn, Dlocation)Redundant (Dname, Dmgr_ssn repeated); later 2NF splits it into technique 1 anyway.
    3. Fixed number of columnsDlocation1, Dlocation2, Dlocation3 (if at most 3 are known)Avoid: NULLs, a false ordering, awkward queries (“departments located in Bellaire”).

    Nested relations are unnested the same way, propagating the key: EMP_PROJ(Ssn, Ename, {PROJS(Pnumber, Hours)}) becomes EMP_PROJ1(Ssn, Ename) and EMP_PROJ2(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours). With two independent multivalued attributes (PERSON(Ss#, {Car_lic#}, {Phone#})) use technique 1 twice; technique 2 would create an all-key relation with an MVD (see 4NF).

    2NF and 3NF based on the primary key

    Definition: 2NF and 3NF (primary key only, Codd)

    2NF: every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (no partial dependency). If the primary key is a single attribute, the relation is automatically in 2NF.

    3NF: 2NF, and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key (no non-key attribute or set of non-key attributes determines another non-key attribute).

    EMP_PROJ to 2NF, EMP_DEPT to 3NF

    EMP_PROJ(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Ename, Pname, Plocation), FD1 {Ssn,Pnumber}→Hours\{\textsf{Ssn},\textsf{Pnumber}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Hours}{Ssn,Pnumber}→Hours, FD2 Ssn→Ename\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \textsf{Ename}Ssn→Ename, FD3 Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation}\textsf{Pnumber} \rightarrow \{\textsf{Pname},\textsf{Plocation}\}Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation}. Key {Ssn,Pnumber}\{\textsf{Ssn},\textsf{Pnumber}\}{Ssn,Pnumber}; FD2 and FD3 are partial (LHS is a proper subset of the key, RHS non-prime), so not 2NF. Each non-prime attribute goes with the part of the key it fully depends on: EP1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours), EP2(Ssn, Ename), EP3(Pnumber, Pname, Plocation).

    EMP_DEPT(Ename, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn) with Ssn→{Ename,Bdate,Address,Dnumber}\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \{\textsf{Ename},\textsf{Bdate},\textsf{Address},\textsf{Dnumber}\}Ssn→{Ename,Bdate,Address,Dnumber} and Dnumber→{Dname,Dmgr_ssn}\textsf{Dnumber} \rightarrow \{\textsf{Dname},\textsf{Dmgr\_ssn}\}Dnumber→{Dname,Dmgr_ssn}. The key is the single attribute Ssn, so 2NF holds. Dnumber is non-key and determines Dname and Dmgr_ssn (transitive: Ssn→Dnumber→Dmgr_ssn\textsf{Ssn}\to \textsf{Dnumber}\to \textsf{Dmgr\_ssn}Ssn→Dnumber→Dmgr_ssn), so not 3NF. Decompose: ED1(Ename, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Dnumber) and ED2(Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn).

    General definitions (all candidate keys)

    The primary-key versions ignore the other candidate keys. The general definitions use every candidate key, and “prime” means “in some candidate key”.

    Definition: General 2NF, 3NF and BCNF
    • 2NF: no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key (every non-prime attribute is fully dependent on every key).
    • 3NF: for every non-trivial FD X→AX \rightarrow AX→A that holds in RRR (i.e. in F+F^+F+), (a) XXX is a superkey of RRR, or (b) AAA is a prime attribute of RRR.
    • BCNF: for every non-trivial FD X→AX \rightarrow AX→A in F+F^+F+, XXX is a superkey of RRR. (3NF without escape clause (b).)

    Alternative 3NF definition: every non-prime attribute is (i) fully functionally dependent on every key and (ii) non-transitively dependent on every key.

    Reading the general 3NF test

    A violation is an FD X→AX \rightarrow AX→A with XXX not a superkey and AAA non-prime. Two shapes:

    • XXX is a proper subset of a key: a partial dependency (this also breaks 2NF);
    • XXX is not contained in any key (it contains a non-prime attribute): a transitive dependency (breaks 3NF only).

    So general 3NF implies general 2NF; you may test 3NF directly. BCNF ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ 3NF ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ 2NF ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ 1NF.

    It is enough to test the given FDs (with split right sides)

    To check 3NF/BCNF of the original RRR against a given FFF, it suffices to check the FDs of FFF after splitting right sides into single attributes: if every X→A∈FX \rightarrow A\in FX→A∈F passes, every FD in F+F^+F+ passes. But for a piece RiR_iRi​ of a decomposition you must use the projected FDs: for each X⊆RiX\subseteq R_iX⊆Ri​, look at X+∩RiX^+\cap R_iX+∩Ri​ (computed with the full FFF). An FD that “crosses” pieces can create an FD inside a piece that is not written in FFF.

    LOTS (Figure 14.12): general 2NF and 3NF

    LOTS(Property_id#, County_name, Lot#, Area, Price, Tax_rate) with

    FD1 Property_id#→all others\textsf{Property\_id\#} \rightarrow \text{all others}Property_id#→all others; FD2 {County_name,Lot#}→{Property_id#,Area,Price,Tax_rate}\{\textsf{County\_name},\textsf{Lot\#}\} \rightarrow \{\textsf{Property\_id\#},\textsf{Area},\textsf{Price},\textsf{Tax\_rate}\}{County_name,Lot#}→{Property_id#,Area,Price,Tax_rate}; FD3 County_name→Tax_rate\textsf{County\_name} \rightarrow \textsf{Tax\_rate}County_name→Tax_rate; FD4 Area→Price\textsf{Area} \rightarrow \textsf{Price}Area→Price.

    Candidate keys: Property_id# and {County_name, Lot#}. Prime: Property_id#, County_name, Lot#. Non-prime: Area, Price, Tax_rate.

    2NF: FD3 makes non-prime Tax_rate depend on County_name ⊂\subset⊂ {County_name, Lot#}: partial, so LOTS is not in 2NF (judged on the primary key Property_id# alone it would look 2NF, which is why the general definition matters). Split: LOTS1(Property_id#, County_name, Lot#, Area, Price), LOTS2(County_name, Tax_rate).

    3NF: in LOTS1, FD4 Area→Price\textsf{Area} \rightarrow \textsf{Price}Area→Price violates 3NF because Area is not a superkey and Price is non-prime. Split: LOTS1A(Property_id#, County_name, Lot#, Area), LOTS1B(Area, Price). Result: LOTS1A, LOTS1B, LOTS2, all in 3NF. Testing LOTS against general 3NF directly finds FD3 and FD4 at once.

    Boyce–Codd normal form

    BCNF removes clause (b) of 3NF. A relation is in 3NF but not BCNF exactly when some FD X→AX \rightarrow AX→A holds with XXX not a superkey but AAA prime. The standard pattern (Figure 14.13(b)) is R(A‾,B‾,C)R(\underline{A},\underline{B},C)R(A​,B​,C) with AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C and C→BC \rightarrow BC→B.

    TEACH: in 3NF but not BCNF (Figure 14.14)

    TEACH(Student, Course, Instructor) with FD1 {Student,Course}→Instructor\{\textsf{Student},\textsf{Course}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Instructor}{Student,Course}→Instructor and FD2 Instructor→Course\textsf{Instructor} \rightarrow \textsf{Course}Instructor→Course (each instructor teaches one course).

    • Closures: {S,C}+=SCI\{S,C\}^+=SCI{S,C}+=SCI (FD1); {S,I}+=SIC\{S,I\}^+=SIC{S,I}+=SIC (FD2); S+=SS^+=SS+=S, C+=CC^+=CC+=C, I+=ICI^+=ICI+=IC. Candidate keys: {S,C}\{S,C\}{S,C} and {S,I}\{S,I\}{S,I} (minimal: no single attribute is a superkey). All three attributes are prime.
    • 3NF: FD1 has a superkey LHS; FD2 has RHS Course, which is prime. So 3NF holds.
    • BCNF: FD2’s LHS Instructor is not a superkey (I+=IC≠RI^+=IC\neq RI+=IC=R). So not BCNF. Redundancy: “Mark teaches Database” is repeated for every student of Mark.

    • Decompositions into two relations, tested with NJB (Section 6.3):

      OptionR1∩R2R_1\cap R_2R1​∩R2​R1−R2R_1-R_2R1​−R2​R2−R1R_2-R_1R2​−R1​Lossless?
      {S,I},{S,C}\{S,I\},\{S,C\}{S,I},{S,C}SSSIIICCCno (S+=SS^+=SS+=S)
      {C,I},{C,S}\{C,I\},\{C,S\}{C,I},{C,S}CCCIIISSSno (C+=CC^+=CC+=C)
      {I,C},{I,S}\{I,C\},\{I,S\}{I,C},{I,S}IIICCCSSSyes (I→CI \rightarrow CI→C)
    • BCNF answer: TEACH1(Instructor, Course), TEACH2(Student, Instructor). FD1 is lost: no relation contains Student, Course and Instructor together. This is the standard example of BCNF costing a dependency.

    Multivalued dependencies and 4NF

    EMP(Ename, Pname, Dname): an employee has several projects and, independently, several dependents. To avoid implying a link between a project and a dependent, every combination must be stored (Smith with projects X, Y and dependents John, Anna needs 4 tuples). EMP is all-key, has no non-trivial FDs, so it is in BCNF, yet it is redundant.

    Definition: Multivalued dependency and 4NF

    X↠YX \twoheadrightarrow YX↠Y holds on RRR (with Z=R−(X∪Y)Z=R-(X\cup Y)Z=R−(X∪Y)) if whenever t1,t2∈rt_1,t_2\in rt1​,t2​∈r with t1[X]=t2[X]t_1[X]=t_2[X]t1​[X]=t2​[X], there are t3,t4∈rt_3,t_4\in rt3​,t4​∈r with t3[X]=t4[X]=t1[X]t_3[X]=t_4[X]=t_1[X]t3​[X]=t4​[X]=t1​[X], t3[Y]=t1[Y]t_3[Y]=t_1[Y]t3​[Y]=t1​[Y], t3[Z]=t2[Z]t_3[Z]=t_2[Z]t3​[Z]=t2​[Z], t4[Y]=t2[Y]t_4[Y]=t_2[Y]t4​[Y]=t2​[Y], t4[Z]=t1[Z]t_4[Z]=t_1[Z]t4​[Z]=t1​[Z]. By symmetry X↠YX \twoheadrightarrow YX↠Y implies X↠ZX \twoheadrightarrow ZX↠Z, written X↠Y∣ZX\twoheadrightarrow Y\mid ZX↠Y∣Z. The MVD is trivial if Y⊆XY\subseteq XY⊆X or X∪Y=RX\cup Y=RX∪Y=R.

    4NF: for every non-trivial MVD X↠YX \twoheadrightarrow YX↠Y in F+F^+F+, XXX is a superkey. Every FD is also an MVD (replication rule), so 4NF ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ BCNF.

    MVDs arise when two independent 1:N facts about XXX are put in one relation (typically technique 2 of 1NF applied to two multivalued attributes). EMP has Ename↠Pname∣Dname\textsf{Ename}\twoheadrightarrow \textsf{Pname}\mid \textsf{Dname}Ename↠Pname∣Dname and Ename is not a superkey, so EMP is not in 4NF.

    4NF decomposition (Algorithm 15.7). D:={R}D:=\{R\}D:={R}; while some Q∈DQ\in DQ∈D is not in 4NF, pick a non-trivial X↠YX \twoheadrightarrow YX↠Y in QQQ with XXX not a superkey of QQQ, and replace QQQ by (X∪Y)(X\cup Y)(X∪Y) and (Q−Y)(Q-Y)(Q−Y). Each split is lossless by property NJB′'′: {R1,R2}\{R_1,R_2\}{R1​,R2​} is lossless iff (R1∩R2)↠(R1−R2)(R_1\cap R_2)\twoheadrightarrow(R_1-R_2)(R1​∩R2​)↠(R1​−R2​). For EMP with Ename↠Pname\textsf{Ename} \twoheadrightarrow \textsf{Pname}Ename↠Pname: EMP_PROJECTS(Ename, Pname) and EMP_DEPENDENTS(Ename, Dname); in each, the MVD is now trivial. Adding Brown to a new project then takes one tuple instead of one per dependent.

    Join dependencies and 5NF

    Definition: Join dependency and 5NF (PJNF)

    JD(R1,…,Rn)JD(R_1,\dots,R_n)JD(R1​,…,Rn​) holds on RRR if every legal state satisfies ∗(πR1(r),…,πRn(r))=r*\big(\pi_{R_1}(r),\dots,\pi_{R_n}(r)\big)=r∗(πR1​​(r),…,πRn​​(r))=r. It is trivial if some Ri=RR_i=RRi​=R. An MVD is the case n=2n=2n=2. RRR is in 5NF (project-join normal form) if for every non-trivial JD in F+F^+F+, every RiR_iRi​ is a superkey of RRR.

    Example (SUPPLY(Sname, Part_name, Proj_name), all-key, in 4NF): rule “if sss supplies ppp, project jjj uses ppp, and sss supplies at least one part to jjj, then sss supplies ppp to jjj” is JD(R1,R2,R3)JD(R_1,R_2,R_3)JD(R1​,R2​,R3​) with R1R_1R1​(Sname, Part_name), R2R_2R2​(Sname, Proj_name), R3R_3R3​(Part_name, Proj_name). Joining any two projections of the 7-tuple state of Figure 14.15(c) gives spurious tuples (e.g. R1∗R2R_1*R_2R1​∗R2​ adds (Smith, Nut, ProjX) and (Adamsky, Nail, ProjY)), but joining all three gives back exactly SUPPLY. JDs are hard to discover, so 5NF is rarely used in practice. Date and Fagin: a 3NF schema whose keys are all single attributes is in 5NF.

    5  Inference rules, closures and keys · Ch. 15.1

    Theory recap

    Armstrong’s axioms and derived rules

    F⊨X→YF\models X \rightarrow YF⊨X→Y means X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y holds in every state that satisfies FFF. F+F^+F+, the closure of FFF, is the set of all FDs implied by FFF.

    Definition: Inference rules (write XYXYXY for X∪YX\cup YX∪Y)
    IR1reflexiveif Y⊆XY\subseteq XY⊆X then X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y
    IR2augmentation{X→Y}⊨XZ→YZ\{X \rightarrow Y\}\models XZ \rightarrow YZ{X→Y}⊨XZ→YZ

    IR1–IR3 (Armstrong’s axioms) are sound (everything derived holds in every state satisfying FFF) and complete (everything in F+F^+F+ can be derived with them). IR4–IR6 follow from IR1–IR3.

    Proofs of IR1–IR3 from the definition.

    • IR1. Let Y⊆XY\subseteq XY⊆X and t1[X]=t2[X]t_1[X]=t_2[X]t1​[X]=t2​[X]. Since Y⊆XY\subseteq XY⊆X, t1[Y]=t2[Y]t_1[Y]=t_2[Y]t1​[Y]=t2​[Y]. So X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y holds in every state.
    • IR2 (contradiction). Suppose X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y holds in rrr but XZ→YZXZ \rightarrow YZXZ→YZ fails: some t1,t2t_1,t_2t1​,t2​ have (1) t1[XZ]=t2[XZ]t_1[XZ]=t_2[XZ]t1​[XZ]=t2​[XZ] and (2) t1[YZ]≠t2[YZ]t_1[YZ]\neq t_2[YZ]t1​[YZ]=t2​[YZ]. From (1), t1[X]=t2[X]t_1[X]=t_2[X]t1​[X]=t2​[X] and t1[Z]=t2[Z]t_1[Z]=t_2[Z]t1​[Z]=t2​[Z]. By X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y, t1[Y]=t2[Y]t_1[Y]=t_2[Y]t1​[Y]=t2​[Y]. Hence t1[YZ]=t2[YZ]t_1[YZ]=t_2[YZ]t1​[YZ]=t2​[YZ], contradicting (2).
    • IR3. Let t1[X]=t2[X]t_1[X]=t_2[X]t1​[X]=t2​[X]. By X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y, t1[Y]=t2[Y]t_1[Y]=t_2[Y]t1​[Y]=t2​[Y]; by Y→ZY \rightarrow ZY→Z, t1[Z]=t2[Z]t_1[Z]=t_2[Z]t1​[Z]=t2​[Z].

    Proofs of IR4–IR6 from IR1–IR3.

    • IR4. X→YZX \rightarrow YZX→YZ (given); YZ→YYZ \rightarrow YYZ→Y (IR1, Y⊆YZY\subseteq YZY⊆YZ); so X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y (IR3).
    • IR5. (1) X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y, (2) X→ZX \rightarrow ZX→Z given. Augment (1) with XXX: X→XYX \rightarrow XYX→XY (IR2, XX=XXX=XXX=X). Augment (2) with YYY: XY→YZXY \rightarrow YZXY→YZ (IR2). Then X→YZX \rightarrow YZX→YZ (IR3).
    • IR6. Augment X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y with WWW: WX→WYWX \rightarrow WYWX→WY (IR2). With WY→ZWY \rightarrow ZWY→Z, IR3 gives WX→ZWX \rightarrow ZWX→Z.
    Rules that do not exist

    XY→ZXY \rightarrow ZXY→Z does not give X→ZX \rightarrow ZX→Z; X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y does not give Y→XY \rightarrow XY→X. Only the RHS may be split (IR4).

    Attribute closure (Algorithm 15.1)

    Definition: Closure of an attribute set

    X+={A∣F⊨X→A}X^+=\{A\mid F\models X \rightarrow A\}X+={A∣F⊨X→A}. Fact: X→Y∈F+  ⟺  Y⊆X+X \rightarrow Y\in F^+\iff Y\subseteq X^+X→Y∈F+⟺Y⊆X+. So XXX is a superkey iff X+=RX^+=RX+=R.

    X+ := X
repeat
    old := X+
    for each FD  Y -> Z  in F:
        if Y is a subset of X+ then X+ := X+ union Z
until X+ = old

    Finding all candidate keys

    Systematic method

    Classify each attribute by where it appears in FFF (right sides split):

    1. On no RHS (only LHS, or in no FD at all): in every key. (Proof: pattern (v) in Section 8.) Call this set Core\mathit{Core}Core.
    2. Only on the RHS (never on a LHS): in no key. (It never helps determine anything else, so removing it from a superkey leaves a superkey, because it is re-derived from the others.)
    3. Middle (on both sides): test. If Core+=R\mathit{Core}^+=RCore+=R, Core\mathit{Core}Core is the only key. Otherwise try Core\mathit{Core}Core plus 1 middle attribute, then plus 2, …; skip any set that contains a key already found (it would not be minimal).

    Algorithm 15.2(a) (start with K:=RK:=RK:=R, drop each attribute whose removal keeps K+=RK^+=RK+=R) finds one key only.

    Running example: all keys

    RHS attributes: CCC (AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C), B,D,EB,D,EB,D,E (C→BDEC \rightarrow BDEC→BDE), EEE, FFF. LHS attributes: A,B,C,DA,B,C,DA,B,C,D.

    • On no RHS: AAA ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ AAA is in every key. Only on RHS: E,FE,FE,F ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ in no key. Middle: B,C,DB,C,DB,C,D.
    • A+=A≠RA^+=A\neq RA+=A=R, so add middle attributes one at a time: (AB)+=R(AB)^+=R(AB)+=R ✓, (AC)+=R(AC)^+=R(AC)+=R ✓, (AD)+=ADE(AD)^+=ADE(AD)+=ADE ×.
    • Two middle attributes: ABC,ABDABC, ABDABC,ABD contain ABABAB; ACDACDACD contains ACACAC: none can be minimal. Done.
    • Minimality: ABABAB and ACACAC are superkeys and their proper subsets AAA, BBB, CCC have closures AAA, BBB, BCDEBCDEBCDE, none equal to RRR.

    Keys: ABABAB and ACACAC. Prime: A,B,CA,B,CA,B,C. Non-prime: D,E,FD,E,FD,E,F.

    Running example: highest normal form
    • 1NF: yes (assume atomic attributes).
    • 2NF: fails. C→DEC \rightarrow DEC→DE (from C→BDEC \rightarrow BDEC→BDE): C⊂ACC\subset ACC⊂AC (a proper subset of a key) and D,ED,ED,E are non-prime: partial dependency.
    • (3NF would also fail: D→ED \rightarrow ED→E, DDD not a superkey, EEE non-prime: transitive AB→C→D→EAB\to C\to D\to EAB→C→D→E.)
    Answer

    Keys ABABAB, ACACAC; highest normal form 1NF.

    Equivalence and covers

    Definition: Cover, equivalence

    FFF covers EEE if every FD of EEE is in F+F^+F+. EEE and FFF are equivalent (E≡FE\equiv FE≡F, E+=F+E^+=F^+E+=F+) if each covers the other. Test: for each X→Y∈EX \rightarrow Y\in EX→Y∈E compute X+X^+X+ under FFF and check Y⊆X+Y\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+; then the other direction.

    Book exercise: F={A→C,AC→D,E→AD,E→H}F=\{A \rightarrow C,AC \rightarrow D,E \rightarrow AD,E \rightarrow H\}F={A→C,AC→D,E→AD,E→H}, G={A→CD,E→AH}G=\{A \rightarrow CD,E \rightarrow AH\}G={A→CD,E→AH}

    GGG covers FFF: under GGG, A+=ACD⊇CA^+=ACD\supseteq CA+=ACD⊇C; (AC)+=ACD⊇D(AC)^+=ACD\supseteq D(AC)+=ACD⊇D; E+=ACDEH⊇AD,HE^+=ACDEH\supseteq AD, HE+=ACDEH⊇AD,H. FFF covers GGG: under FFF, A+=ACD⊇CDA^+=ACD\supseteq CDA+=ACD⊇CD; E+=ACDEH⊇AHE^+=ACDEH\supseteq AHE+=ACDEH⊇AH. Hence F≡GF\equiv GF≡G.

    Minimal cover (Algorithm 15.2)

    Definition: Minimal set of FDs

    FFF is minimal if (1) every RHS is a single attribute; (2) no X→AX \rightarrow AX→A can be replaced by Y→AY \rightarrow AY→A with Y⊂XY\subset XY⊂X and still be equivalent (no extraneous LHS attribute); (3) no FD can be removed and still be equivalent (no redundant FD). A minimal cover of EEE is a minimal set equivalent to EEE. One always exists.

    1. Split every RHS:  X -> A1..An   becomes   X -> A1, ..., X -> An.
2. For each X -> A with |X| > 1, for each B in X:
       B is extraneous  iff  A is in (X - B)+   (closure under the CURRENT set)
       if so replace X -> A by (X - B) -> A.
3. For each remaining X -> A (one at a time, on the CURRENT set):
       X -> A is redundant  iff  A is in X+ computed WITHOUT X -> A
       if so delete it.

    ABD→FABD \rightarrow FABD→F: drop AAA: (BD)+=BDE∌F(BD)^+=BDE\not\ni F(BD)+=BDE∋F; drop BBB: (AD)+=ADE∌F(AD)^+=ADE\not\ni F(AD)+=ADE∋F; drop DDD: (AB)+=ABCDEF∋F(AB)^+=ABCDEF\ni F(AB)+=ABCDEF∋F. So DDD is extraneous; replace by AB→FAB \rightarrow FAB→F.

Check: under GGG, (AB)+=R(AB)^+=R(AB)+=R, C+=BCDEC^+=BCDEC+=BCDE, D+=DED^+=DED+=DE, so every FD of FFF is recovered and G≡FG\equiv FG≡F.

    Minimal covers are not unique; test against the current set

    The result depends on the order of tests. With F={A→B,B→A,A→C,B→C}F=\{A \rightarrow B,B \rightarrow A,A \rightarrow C,B \rightarrow C\}F={A→B,B→A,A→C,B→C}, testing A→CA \rightarrow CA→C first removes it (via A→B→CA\to B\to CA→B→C) and then B→CB \rightarrow CB→C is essential; testing B→CB \rightarrow CB→C first gives the other answer. Both {A→B,B→A,B→C}\{A \rightarrow B,B \rightarrow A,B \rightarrow C\}{A→B,B→A,B→C} and {A→B,B→A,A→C}\{A \rightarrow B,B \rightarrow A,A \rightarrow C\}{A→B,B→A,A→C} are minimal covers. Two FDs may each be redundant on their own but not both together: after deleting one, re-test the next against the reduced set. Do step 2 for all FDs before step 3 (removing a redundant FD first can hide an extraneous attribute).

    6  Properties of decompositions · Ch. 15.2

    Theory recap

    A decomposition of RRR is D={R1,…,Rm}D=\{R_1,\dots,R_m\}D={R1​,…,Rm​} with Ri⊆RR_i\subseteq RRi​⊆R. Each RiR_iRi​ being in BCNF or 3NF is not enough: EMP_LOCS(Ename, Plocation) is in BCNF (two attributes) yet joining it with EMP_PROJ1 gives spurious tuples. Three properties of DDD as a whole matter.

    Attribute preservation

    ⋃iRi=R\bigcup_{i} R_i=R⋃i​Ri​=R: every attribute appears in some relation.

    Dependency preservation

    Definition: Projection of FFF and dependency preservation

    πRi(F)={X→Y∈F+∣X∪Y⊆Ri}\pi_{R_i}(F)=\{X \rightarrow Y\in F^+\mid X\cup Y\subseteq R_i\}πRi​​(F)={X→Y∈F+∣X∪Y⊆Ri​} (taken from F+F^+F+, not just FFF). DDD is dependency-preserving if (πR1(F)∪⋯∪πRm(F))+=F+\big(\pi_{R_1}(F)\cup\dots\cup\pi_{R_m}(F)\big)^+=F^+(πR1​​(F)∪⋯∪πRm​​(F))+=F+. An FD that lives in no single relation can be enforced only by joining relations on every update.

    Test without computing F+F^+F+. For each X→Y∈FX \rightarrow Y\in FX→Y∈F: set Z:=XZ:=XZ:=X; repeat, for each RiR_iRi​, Z:=Z∪((Z∩Ri)+∩Ri)Z:=Z\cup\big((Z\cap R_i)^+\cap R_i\big)Z:=Z∪((Z∩Ri​)+∩Ri​) (closure under FFF), until ZZZ stops changing. The FD is preserved iff Y⊆ZY\subseteq ZY⊆Z. In an exam it is usually enough to show each FD of a (minimal) cover lies inside some RiR_iRi​, or follows from FDs that do.

    Lossless (nonadditive) join

    Definition: Lossless join

    DDD has the lossless (nonadditive) join property w.r.t. FFF if for every state rrr satisfying FFF, ∗(πR1(r),…,πRm(r))=r*\big(\pi_{R_1}(r),\dots,\pi_{R_m}(r)\big)=r∗(πR1​​(r),…,πRm​​(r))=r. “Loss” means loss of information: a lossy join returns extra (spurious) tuples, never fewer. This property is a must; dependency preservation is desirable but may be sacrificed.

    NJB: binary test

    {R1,R2}\{R_1,R_2\}{R1​,R2​} is lossless w.r.t. FFF iff

    (R1∩R2)→(R1−R2)∈F+or(R1∩R2)→(R2−R1)∈F+.(R_1\cap R_2)\to(R_1-R_2)\in F^+\qquad\text{or}\qquad (R_1\cap R_2)\to(R_2-R_1)\in F^+ .(R1​∩R2​)→(R1​−R2​)∈F+or(R1​∩R2​)→(R2​−R1​)∈F+.

    Compute (R1∩R2)+(R_1\cap R_2)^+(R1​∩R2​)+: lossless iff it contains all of R1R_1R1​ or all of R2R_2R2​, i.e. the common attributes are a superkey of one side.

    Claim 2 (successive splits): if DDD is lossless and some RiR_iRi​ is split losslessly (w.r.t. πRi(F)\pi_{R_i}(F)πRi​​(F)), the new decomposition is still lossless. So a chain of NJB-lossless binary splits is lossless.

    NJB on the running example

    {ABDF, CDE}\{ABDF,\ CDE\}{ABDF, CDE}: common DDD, D+=DED^+=DED+=DE; R1−R2=ABFR_1-R_2=ABFR1​−R2​=ABF, R2−R1=CER_2-R_1=CER2​−R1​=CE; D+D^+D+ contains neither: lossy.
    {ACF, BCDE}\{ACF,\ BCDE\}{ACF, BCDE}: common CCC, C+=BCDE⊇BCDEC^+=BCDE\supseteq BCDEC+=BCDE⊇BCDE: lossless (CCC is a key of BCDEBCDEBCDE).

    The general chase test (Algorithm 15.3) for any number of relations:

    1. Matrix S: one row per R_i, one column per attribute A_j of R.
2. S(i,j) := a_j  if A_j is in R_i,   else  b_ij  (a distinct symbol).
3. Repeat until a full pass changes nothing:
     for each FD X -> Y in F:
       for rows that agree on all columns of X:
         make them agree on each column of Y:
           if one of them has an a-symbol there, set all to that a-symbol,
           else set all to one of their b-symbols.
4. Lossless  iff  some row becomes all a-symbols (you may stop as soon as one does).

    The matrix is a state satisfying FFF; a row of all aaa’s is a tuple of the join that must already be in rrr. If no row becomes all aaa’s, the final matrix is a counterexample state.

    7  Design algorithms · Ch. 15.3–15.4

    Theory recap
    What each algorithm guarantees

    3NF synthesis (15.4): lossless and dependency-preserving, every relation in 3NF.

    BCNF decomposition (15.5): lossless, every relation in BCNF, dependency preservation not guaranteed.

    You cannot always have all three of: lossless, dependency-preserving, BCNF. Lossless is never given up.

    3NF synthesis (Algorithm 15.4)

    1. Find a minimal cover G of F.
2. For each LHS X in G, make one relation  X u {A1,...,Ak}  where X->A1..X->Ak are all
   the FDs of G with left side X.   (X is a key of that relation.)
3. If no relation contains a candidate key of R, add one relation that is a key of R.
4. Remove any relation that is a projection of (contained in) another relation.

    Step 2 puts every FD of GGG inside one relation (dependency preservation); step 3 makes the key-relation’s row become all aaa’s in the chase (lossless).

    3NF synthesis on the running example

    Step 1

    Minimal cover G={AB→CF, C→BD, D→E}G=\{AB \rightarrow CF,\ C \rightarrow BD,\ D \rightarrow E\}G={AB→CF, C→BD, D→E} (computed above).

    Step 2: one relation per left side

    S1(A,B‾,C,F)S_1(\underline{A,B},C,F)S1​(A,B​,C,F) from AB→CFAB \rightarrow CFAB→CF;  S2(C‾,B,D)S_2(\underline{C},B,D)S2​(C​,B,D) from C→BDC \rightarrow BDC→BD;  S3(D‾,E)S_3(\underline{D},E)S3​(D​,E) from D→ED \rightarrow ED→E.

    Step 3: key present?

    S1S_1S1​ contains ABABAB, a key of RRR: nothing added.

    Step 4: contained relations

    None of S1,S2,S3S_1,S_2,S_3S1​,S2​,S3​ is a subset of another: nothing removed.

    Checks

    S1S_1S1​: projected FDs AB→CFAB \rightarrow CFAB→CF, C→BC \rightarrow BC→B, AC→FAC \rightarrow FAC→F; keys ABABAB, ACACAC. C→BC \rightarrow BC→B: CCC is not a superkey of S1S_1S1​ but BBB is prime, so S1S_1S1​ is in 3NF but not BCNF. S2S_2S2​ (key CCC) and S3S_3S3​ (key DDD) are in BCNF.

    Answer

    {S1(A,B‾,C,F), S2(C‾,B,D), S3(D‾,E)}\{S_1(\underline{A,B},C,F),\ S_2(\underline{C},B,D),\ S_3(\underline{D},E)\}{S1​(A,B​,C,F), S2​(C​,B,D), S3​(D​,E)}: all 3NF, lossless (S1S_1S1​ contains the key ABABAB), dependency-preserving (each FD of GGG lies in one relation).

    BCNF decomposition (Algorithm 15.5)

    D := {R}
while some Q in D is not in BCNF:
    find a non-trivial X -> Y holding in Q with X not a superkey of Q
       (use closures: Y := (X+ intersect Q) - X  is the usual choice)
    replace Q by  (X u Y)  and  (Q - Y)

    Each split is lossless by NJB (the common part XXX determines X∪YX\cup YX∪Y, so XXX is a key of the first piece), and by Claim 2 the whole result is lossless.

    FDs in R1R_1R1​: C→BDEC \rightarrow BDEC→BDE, D→ED \rightarrow ED→E; key CCC; D+∩R1=DE≠R1D^+\cap R_1=DE\neq R_1D+∩R1​=DE=R1​: not BCNF.
    FDs in R2R_2R2​: (AC)+∩R2=ACF(AC)^+\cap R_2=ACF(AC)+∩R2​=ACF, so AC→FAC \rightarrow FAC→F; A+=AA^+=AA+=A, C+∩R2=CC^+\cap R_2=CC+∩R2​=C, F+=FF^+=FF+=F; key ACACAC: BCNF. Lossless: R1∩R2=CR_1\cap R_2=CR1​∩R2​=C is a key of R1R_1R1​.

    Split 2: R1(B,C,D,E)R_1(B,C,D,E)R1​(B,C,D,E) on D→ED \rightarrow ED→E

    Answer

    {R3(D‾,E), R4(C‾,B,D), R2(A,C‾,F)}\{R_3(\underline{D},E),\ R_4(\underline{C},B,D),\ R_2(\underline{A,C},F)\}{R3​(D​,E), R4​(C​,B,D), R2​(A,C​,F)}, every relation in BCNF, lossless (chase above). Lost: AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C (and with it AB→FAB \rightarrow FAB→F): with Z:=ABZ:=ABZ:=AB, no relation adds anything (B+∩R4=BB^+\cap R_4=BB+∩R4​=B, A+∩R2=AA^+\cap R_2=AA+∩R2​=A), so C∉ZC\notin ZC∈/Z.

    Common BCNF mistakes

    Making “one relation per FD” without re-checking each piece; forgetting derived FDs inside a piece; splitting a relation that is already in BCNF; ending with no relation that holds a key of RRR (lossy). Another order (e.g. splitting on D→ED \rightarrow ED→E first) may give a different but equally correct answer.

    Why BCNF may lose dependencies

    Whenever some FD X→AX \rightarrow AX→A has XXX not a superkey and AAA prime, splitting on it separates the attributes of the key that contains AAA. Pattern: R(A,B,C)R(A,B,C)R(A,B,C) with AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C, C→BC \rightarrow BC→B. Keys ABABAB, ACACAC; 3NF yes; BCNF no (CCC not a superkey). The only lossless BCNF split is {(C,B),(A,C)}\{(C,B),(A,C)\}{(C,B),(A,C)}, and AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C lies in neither relation. Any BCNF decomposition must separate A,B,CA,B,CA,B,C (all of RRR is not BCNF), so no BCNF decomposition preserves AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C. TEACH and LOTS1A (with Area→County_name\textsf{Area} \rightarrow \textsf{County\_name}Area→County_name, which loses {County,Lot#}→Property_id\{\textsf{County},\textsf{Lot\#}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Property\_id}{County,Lot#}→Property_id) are instances of this pattern. In practice, either stay in 3NF (keeping the FD) or go to BCNF and enforce the lost FD by other means.

    NULLs and dangling tuples (Ch. 15.4)

    • Lossless-join theory assumes join attributes are never NULL. An employee with NULL Dnum disappears from EMPLOYEE ∗*∗ DEPARTMENT; a LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps such tuples.
    • Dangling tuples: over-decomposing EMPLOYEE into EMPLOYEE_1(Ssn, Ename, …) and EMPLOYEE_3(Ssn, Dnum) that omits employees without a department leaves tuples of EMPLOYEE_1 with no partner; a natural join silently drops them.
    • Normalization algorithms also depend on the FDs being complete and are not deterministic (order of tests, choice of minimal cover).

    Normal forms at a glance

    NFCondition (general)ForbidsRemedy
    1NFatomic, single-valued attributesmultivalued/composite attributes, nested relationsnew relation per multivalued attribute (technique 1)
    2NFno non-prime attribute partially dependent on any keyproper subset of a key →\to→ non-primeput the subset with the attributes it determines in a new relation
    3NFevery non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A: XXX superkey or AAA primepartial and transitive dependencies of non-prime attributessplit on the violating FD; or synthesis (15.4)
    BCNFevery non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A: XXX superkeyany FD with a non-superkey LHS, even with prime RHSsplit XYXYXY, R−(Y−X)R-(Y-X)R−(Y−X) (15.5); may lose FDs
    4NFevery non-trivial X↠YX \twoheadrightarrow YX↠Y: XXX superkeyindependent multivalued facts in one relationsplit XYXYXY, R−YR-YR−Y (15.7)
    5NFevery non-trivial JD: each RiR_iRi​ a superkeyjoin dependencies not implied by keysmultiway decomposition

    Each form implies the ones above it. Practical designs aim at 3NF or BCNF (sometimes 4NF).

    8  Proof patterns that past papers asked

    Theory recap

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Attributes are atomic and the given FDs are the complete specification; keys are judged by F+F^+F+, not by sample data. Why: the normal-form definitions are stated over F+F^+F+.
    2. Left-hand sides are non-empty. Why: ∅→Y\emptyset\to Y∅→Y would make YYY constant over the whole relation.
    (i) Any relation schema with two attributes is in BCNF (Ex. 14.22)

    Proof. Let R={A,B}R=\{A,B\}R={A,B} and let X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y be any non-trivial FD holding in RRR, so X≠∅X\neq\emptysetX=∅, X,Y⊆{A,B}X,Y\subseteq\{A,B\}X,Y⊆{A,B} and Y⊈XY\not\subseteq XY⊆X.

    1. X≠{A,B}X\neq\{A,B\}X={A,B}: otherwise Y⊆XY\subseteq XY⊆X and the FD is trivial. So X={A}X=\{A\}X={A} or X={B}X=\{B\}X={B}.
    2. Case X={A}X=\{A\}X={A}: Y⊈{A}Y\not\subseteq\{A\}Y⊆{A} forces B∈YB\in YB∈Y, so A→BA \rightarrow BA→B holds. Then A+⊇{A,B}=RA^+\supseteq\{A,B\}=RA+⊇{A,B}=R and AAA is a superkey.
    3. Case X={B}X=\{B\}X={B}: symmetrically B→AB \rightarrow AB→A and BBB is a superkey.

    So the LHS of every non-trivial FD is a superkey: RRR is in BCNF. (If no non-trivial FD holds, the condition is vacuous and the key is ABABAB.) Covers all four cases: no FD, A→BA \rightarrow BA→B only, B→AB \rightarrow AB→A only, both. ■\blacksquare■

    (ii) 3NF and every candidate key is a single attribute ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ BCNF (2025 End-Sem Q3)

    Proof (by contradiction). Let RRR be in 3NF with all candidate keys simple. Suppose RRR is not in BCNF. Then some non-trivial FD X→AX \rightarrow AX→A holds (RHS split to one attribute, A∉XA\notin XA∈/X) with XXX not a superkey.

    1. Since RRR is in 3NF and XXX is not a superkey, clause (b) must hold: AAA is prime.
    2. So AAA belongs to some candidate key KKK. Every key is a single attribute, so K={A}K=\{A\}K={A}: AAA itself is a key, A→RA \rightarrow RA→R.
    3. From X→AX \rightarrow AX→A and A→RA \rightarrow RA→R, transitivity (IR3) gives X→RX \rightarrow RX→R: XXX is a superkey.
    4. This contradicts the choice of XXX. Hence every non-trivial FD has a superkey LHS: RRR is in BCNF. ■\blacksquare■

    The only gap between 3NF and BCNF is “XXX not a superkey but AAA prime”; if prime attributes are themselves keys, anything that determines one determines everything.

    (iii) Make AAA a key with one added FD, for any FFF (N-I Q1 pattern)

    Question (reconstructed from the N-I key and rubric): R(A,B,…,H)R(A,B,\dots,H)R(A,B,…,H) has some set FFF of FDs and AAA is in no candidate key. Add one FD so that AAA becomes a candidate key, and prove it works whatever FFF is.

    Answer: add A→KA \rightarrow KA→K, where KKK is any candidate key of RRR under FFF

    1. KKK exists and A∉KA\notin KA∈/K. RRR itself is a superkey (R+=RR^+=RR+=R by IR1) and every superkey contains a minimal one, so a candidate key KKK exists for any FFF. A∉KA\notin KA∈/K because AAA is in no key.
    2. A+=RA^+=RA+=R. Under F′=F∪{A→K}F'=F\cup\{A \rightarrow K\}F′=F∪{A→K}: A→KA \rightarrow KA→K (added) and K→RK \rightarrow RK→R (KKK is a key under F⊆F′F\subseteq F'F⊆F′), so A→RA \rightarrow RA→R by transitivity. AAA is a superkey.
    3. Minimality. {A}\{A\}{A} is a single attribute; its only proper subset is ∅\emptyset∅, which is not a superkey (non-empty LHS). So AAA is a candidate key, not just a superkey.
    4. For any FFF. The argument used only that some key KKK exists and K→RK \rightarrow RK→R, both true for every FFF. ■\blacksquare■
    N-I Q1 rubric

    2 marks for A→KA \rightarrow KA→K with KKK stated to be a key (1 only for A→RA \rightarrow RA→R / A→BCDEFGHA \rightarrow BCDEFGHA→BCDEFGH, which is correct but does not use KKK; 0 for X→AX \rightarrow AX→A, a larger LHS, or A→YA \rightarrow YA→Y with YYY not guaranteed to determine RRR such as A→BA \rightarrow BA→B). 1 for deriving A+=RA^+=RA+=R by transitivity (0.5 if asserted). 1 for minimality (0 if you stop at “superkey”). 1 for “holds for any FFF” with the reason that some key always exists. Answers built on A→RA \rightarrow RA→R score at most 4/5.

    (iv) Make given FDs valid by trimming right sides (2025 End-Sem Q7)

    R(A,B,C,D,E,F)R(A,B,C,D,E,F)R(A,B,C,D,E,F), F={A→B, B→A, AC→D, D→CE}F=\{A \rightarrow B,\ B \rightarrow A,\ AC \rightarrow D,\ D \rightarrow CE\}F={A→B, B→A, AC→D, D→CE}.

    (a) Keys and normal form

    On no RHS: FFF (in every key). Only on RHS: EEE (in no key). Middle: A,B,C,DA,B,C,DA,B,C,D. F+=FF^+=FF+=F; (AF)+=ABF(AF)^+=ABF(AF)+=ABF, (BF)+=ABF(BF)^+=ABF(BF)+=ABF, (CF)+=CF(CF)^+=CF(CF)+=CF, (DF)+=CDEF(DF)^+=CDEF(DF)+=CDEF: none is RRR. (ACF)+(ACF)^+(ACF)+: ACF→A→BABCF→AC→DABCDF→D→CERACF\xrightarrow{A\to B}ABCF\xrightarrow{AC\to D}ABCDF\xrightarrow{D\to CE}RACFA→B​ABCFAC→D​ABCDFD→CE​R. Likewise (ADF)+(ADF)^+(ADF)+: ADF→ABDF→ABCDEFADF\to ABDF\to ABCDEFADF→ABDF→ABCDEF (via D→CED \rightarrow CED→CE); (BCF)+(BCF)^+(BCF)+: BCF→ABCF→⋯=RBCF\to ABCF\to\dots=RBCF→ABCF→⋯=R; (BDF)+=R(BDF)^+=R(BDF)+=R. (ABF)+=ABF(ABF)^+=ABF(ABF)+=ABF, (CDF)+=CDEF(CDF)^+=CDEF(CDF)+=CDEF. Four-attribute sets all contain one of these. Keys: ACFACFACF, ADFADFADF, BCFBCFBCF, BDFBDFBDF; prime A,B,C,D,FA,B,C,D,FA,B,C,D,F; non-prime EEE. D→ED \rightarrow ED→E (from D→CED \rightarrow CED→CE): D⊂ADFD\subset ADFD⊂ADF and EEE is non-prime: partial dependency, so not 2NF. Highest NF: 1NF.

    (b) Trimming method

    X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y is valid iff Y⊆X+Y\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+. To make it valid by deleting as few RHS attributes as possible, keep exactly Y∩X+Y\cap X^+Y∩X+: those attributes are implied (IR4 on X→X+X \rightarrow X^+X→X+), and every attribute of Y−X+Y-X^+Y−X+ is not implied, so it must go.

    FDX+X^+X+KeepRemoveResult
    BD→AEFBD \rightarrow AEFBD→AEFBD→B→AABD→D→CEABCDEBD\xrightarrow{B\to A}ABD\xrightarrow{D\to CE}ABCDEBDB→A​ABDD→CE​ABCDEA,EA,EA,EFFFBD→AEBD \rightarrow AEBD→AE
    AE→BCAE \rightarrow BCAE→BCAE→A→BABEAE\xrightarrow{A\to B}ABEAEA→B​ABEBBBCCCAE→BAE \rightarrow BAE→B
    ABF→DFABF \rightarrow DFABF→DFABFABFABF (no FD adds)FFFDDDABF→FABF \rightarrow FABF→F (valid, trivial)

    None of the three is valid as given.

    (v) An attribute on no right side is in every candidate key (GA4 Problem 1)

    Claim. If AAA appears on the RHS of no FD in FFF (as listed; F+F^+F+ always contains A→AA \rightarrow AA→A), then AAA is in every key.

    Proof. Let KKK be a key and suppose A∉KA\notin KA∈/K. Since KKK is a superkey, A∈K+A\in K^+A∈K+. Run the closure algorithm on KKK: it starts from K∌AK\not\ni AK∋A, and each step adds only attributes from the RHS ZZZ of some Y→Z∈FY \rightarrow Z\in FY→Z∈F. By hypothesis A∉ZA\notin ZA∈/Z for every FD, so the invariant “AAA is not in the current closure” holds at the start and is preserved by every step: A∉K+A\notin K^+A∈/K+. Contradiction. So A∈KA\in KA∈K; as KKK was arbitrary, AAA is in every key (indeed every superkey). ■\blacksquare■

    Examples cannot prove a universal statement; graders give at most 3/10 for “proof by example”.

    9  The normalization exam algorithm

    Theory recap
    Checklist: do every step in writing
    1. Assumptions: atomic attributes (so 1NF); the given FDs are complete; keys from F+F^+F+, not data.
    2. Closures: compute X+X^+X+ for every LHS and every single attribute, as a chain naming each FD used.
    3. Keys: no-RHS attributes are in every key, RHS-only attributes in none; test the middle ones from small to large. Show each key is a superkey (K+=RK^+=RK+=R) and minimal (proper subsets fail).
    4. Prime / non-prime: list both sets.
    5. Normal-form checks with reasons, in order: 2NF (proper subset of a key →\to→ non-prime?), 3NF (non-superkey LHS →\to→ non-prime?), BCNF (any non-superkey LHS?). Name the violating FD and the reason; state the highest NF.
    6. Decompose: BCNF by Algorithm 15.5 (each split: FD used, two pieces, projected FDs with closures, key of each piece), or 3NF by synthesis (minimal cover with every test shown, one relation per LHS, add a key relation if needed, drop contained relations).
    7. Final relations each with its key and the NF it is in.
    8. Lossless: for each split, the common attributes are a key of one side (NJB), or a chase table.
    9. Dependency preservation: check each FD of the cover lies in (or follows from FDs in) one relation; name lost FDs.
    Shortcuts when all LHSs are single attributes

    The closure of a set is then the union of the closures of its members. A relation RiR_iRi​ violates BCNF iff some x∈Rix\in R_ix∈Ri​ has x+∩Rix^+\cap R_ix+∩Ri​ larger than {x}\{x\}{x} but not all of RiR_iRi​; it violates 3NF only if one of the extra attributes is non-prime in RiR_iRi​ (this is how the N-I and GA4 rubrics verify answers quickly).

    10  Chapter 14 review questions

    Textbook exercises

    14.2Update anomaliesE&N Ex. 14.2 · p. 496★ Must-do

    Discuss insertion, deletion, and modification anomalies. Why are they considered bad? Illustrate with examples.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Update anomalies arise when a base relation stores facts about several things together (typically a stored join), so the same fact is repeated in many tuples. Example: EMP_DEPT(Ename, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn), where (Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn) is repeated for every employee of the department.

    SsnDnumberDnameDmgr_ssn
    1234567895Research333445555
    3334455555Research333445555
    6668844445Research333445555
    8886655551Headquarters888665555
    AnomalyDefinitionEMP_DEPT example
    InsertionCannot insert a fact without also inserting (or NULL-padding) an unrelated fact, or must re-enter repeated data consistently.(a) A new employee of dept. 5 must carry Research/333445555 exactly as in the other dept. 5 tuples. (b) A new department with no employees can only be inserted with Ssn NULL, which entity integrity forbids.
    DeletionDeleting one fact unintentionally deletes another.Deleting Borg (the only employee of dept. 1) loses the fact that department 1 is Headquarters managed by 888665555.
    ModificationChanging one fact requires updating many tuples; missing one leaves inconsistent data.A new manager for dept. 5 must be written into every dept. 5 employee tuple; if one is missed, dept. 5 has two managers.

    Similarly in EMP_PROJ(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Ename, Pname, Plocation): a project with no workers cannot be inserted (Ssn is part of the key), deleting the last worker of a project loses the project, and renaming a project means updating every WORKS_ON row for it.

    Why bad: they waste storage (redundancy), make updates expensive and error-prone, risk inconsistency (the database contradicts itself), and cause accidental loss of information. In the normalized design EMPLOYEE(Ssn, …, Dnumber), DEPARTMENT(Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn) each department fact is stored once, so none of the three anomalies occurs. (Guideline 2: design base relations without anomalies; if some are kept for performance, document them and handle them in the update programs.)

    Answer

    Insertion, deletion and modification anomalies are side effects of redundancy: you cannot insert, delete or change one fact independently of others. They waste space, invite inconsistency and lose information, so base relations should be decomposed (normalized) to remove them.

    14.3NULLs and spurious tuplesE&N Ex. 14.3 · p. 496

    Why should NULLs in a relation be avoided as much as possible? Discuss the problem of spurious tuples and how we may prevent it.

    Solution · written for this guide

    NULLs

    • Storage: a “fat” relation with attributes that apply to few tuples wastes space.
    • Meaning is ambiguous: NULL may mean not applicable (Visa_status of a citizen), unknown (a missing birth date) or exists but not recorded (a home phone not on file); one NULL cannot say which.
    • Joins: tuples with NULL join attributes vanish from inner joins; inner and outer joins then give different answers.
    • Aggregates and conditions: COUNT, SUM, AVG ignore NULLs; comparisons with NULL are unknown (three-valued logic), so results can surprise.

    Remedy (Guideline 3): move rarely-applicable attributes to a separate relation, e.g. EMP_OFFICES(Essn, Office_number) holding only employees who have an office.

    Spurious tuples

    Spurious tuples are tuples that appear in the natural join of decomposed relations but were not in the original relation; they represent false information. Example: splitting EMP_PROJ into EMP_LOCS(Ename, Plocation) and EMP_PROJ1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname, Plocation) and joining on Plocation pairs every project at Bellaire with every employee who works at Bellaire, e.g. (123456789, 1, 32.5, ProductX, Bellaire, English). The cause: the join attribute Plocation is neither a primary key nor a foreign key, so it does not identify a unique partner tuple.

    Prevention (Guideline 4): design relations that are joined on (primary key, foreign key) pairs; formally, require the lossless (nonadditive) join property: for a binary split, R1∩R2R_1\cap R_2R1​∩R2​ must functionally determine R1−R2R_1-R_2R1​−R2​ or R2−R1R_2-R_1R2​−R1​ (the common attributes are a key of one side), checked with NJB or the chase (Algorithm 15.3). Here {Plocation}+={Plocation}\{\textsf{Plocation}\}^+=\{\textsf{Plocation}\}{Plocation}+={Plocation}, so the split fails the test.

    Answer

    Avoid NULLs because they waste space, have unclear meaning, and break joins and aggregates. Spurious tuples are wrong tuples created by joining on attributes that are not PK–FK pairs; prevent them by decomposing only losslessly (common attributes are a key of one of the relations).

    14.4Informal design guidelinesE&N Ex. 14.4 · p. 496

    State the informal guidelines for relation schema design that we discussed. Illustrate how violation of these guidelines may be harmful.

    Solution · written for this guide
    GuidelineStatementHarm when violated (example)
    1. Clear semanticsEach relation should be easy to explain; do not mix attributes of several entity/relationship types.EMP_DEPT mixes employees and departments: its meaning is muddled and it leads directly to the anomalies of guideline 2.
    2. No redundancy (no anomalies)Design base relations with no insertion, deletion or modification anomalies; if any remain, document them and make programs handle them.EMP_DEPT: cannot add an empty department; deleting the last employee loses the department; changing a manager needs many updates.
    3. Few NULLsAvoid attributes that are frequently NULL; NULLs should be exceptional.Office_number in EMPLOYEE (15% have offices): wasted space, ambiguous NULL meaning, wrong counts and lost tuples in joins.
    4. No spurious tuplesRelations should be joinable on (PK, FK) pairs so that joins generate no spurious tuples.EMP_LOCS ∗*∗ EMP_PROJ1 on Plocation produces employee–project pairs that never existed: queries return false information.

    The guidelines are informal; normalization (FDs, normal forms, lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition) makes 2 and 4 precise.

    Answer

    Clear semantics; no update anomalies (no redundancy); avoid frequent NULLs; no spurious tuples (join on PK–FK, lossless decompositions). Violations cause confusion, inconsistent updates, wasted space and wrong query results.

    14.5Functional dependency and its sourcesE&N Ex. 14.5 · p. 496

    What is a functional dependency? What are the possible sources of the information that defines the functional dependencies that hold among the attributes of a relation schema?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Definition

    For X,Y⊆RX,Y\subseteq RX,Y⊆R, the FD X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y is a constraint on all legal states rrr of RRR: for any tuples t1,t2∈rt_1,t_2\in rt1​,t2​∈r, t1[X]=t2[X]⇒t1[Y]=t2[Y]t_1[X]=t_2[X]\Rightarrow t_1[Y]=t_2[Y]t1​[X]=t2​[X]⇒t1​[Y]=t2​[Y]. The XXX-value uniquely determines the YYY-value. Example in EMP_PROJ: Ssn→Ename\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \textsf{Ename}Ssn→Ename, Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation}\textsf{Pnumber} \rightarrow \{\textsf{Pname},\textsf{Plocation}\}Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation}, {Ssn,Pnumber}→Hours\{\textsf{Ssn},\textsf{Pnumber}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Hours}{Ssn,Pnumber}→Hours.

    Sources

    • The semantics (meaning) of the attributes, as understood by the designer from the application: requirements documents, business rules and policies (“each instructor teaches one course”), regulations and laws (“{State, Driver_license_number} →\to→ Ssn”), and domain experts / users.
    • Keys declared for the conceptual design (a key determines every attribute) and the structure of the ER model (an entity’s key determines its attributes; a 1:N relationship gives N-side key→1-side key\text{N-side key}\to\text{1-side key}N-side key→1-side key).
    • Inference: further FDs follow from the stated ones by Armstrong’s rules (they form F+F^+F+).

    Not a source: the data currently stored (see 14.6). FDs are properties of the schema and can change if the real world changes (Zip_code →\to→ Area_code once held in the U.S. but no longer does).

    Answer

    An FD X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y says equal XXX-values force equal YYY-values in every legal state. FDs come from the meaning of the data: requirements, business rules, laws and domain experts (plus key constraints and those inferred by Armstrong’s rules), never from a sample state.

    14.6FDs from a relation stateE&N Ex. 14.6 · p. 496

    Why can we not infer a functional dependency automatically from a particular relation state?

    Solution · written for this guide

    An FD must hold in every legal state of RRR, now and in the future, but a given state is one snapshot. If no two tuples violate X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y today, that may be a coincidence of the current data; a later legal insertion could violate it. So:

    • a state can only show that an FD may hold (no violating pair);
    • a state can show for certain that an FD does not hold (one violating pair is a counterexample).

    Example (TEACH state of Figure 14.7):

    TeacherCourseText
    SmithData StructuresBartram
    SmithData ManagementMartin
    HallCompilersHoffman
    BrownData StructuresHorowitz

    Text→Course\textsf{Text} \rightarrow \textsf{Course}Text→Course is not violated here, but we cannot conclude it holds (another course could use Bartram). Teacher→Course\textsf{Teacher} \rightarrow \textsf{Course}Teacher→Course certainly does not hold (Smith teaches two courses), nor does Course→Text\textsf{Course} \rightarrow \textsf{Text}Course→Text (Data Structures has two texts). Deciding which FDs hold requires knowing what the attributes mean.

    Answer

    Because an FD is a constraint on all possible legal states (a property of the schema’s semantics), while a state is one instance: data can refute an FD but never establish it.

    14.7Unnormalized relations; history of normal formsE&N Ex. 14.7 · p. 497

    What does the term unnormalized relation refer to? How did the normal forms develop historically from first normal form up to Boyce-Codd normal form?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Unnormalized relation

    A relation that is not in 1NF: some attribute holds non-atomic values (a set of values, a composite value, or a whole nested relation), e.g. DEPARTMENT(Dname, Dnumber, Dmgr_ssn, Dlocations) with Dlocations ={=\{={Bellaire, Sugarland, Houston}\}}, or EMP_PROJ(Ssn, Ename, {PROJS(Pnumber, Hours)}). (In a looser sense the term is also used for any relation not yet normalized to the desired form.)

    Historical development

    1. 1NF (Codd, 1970/72): attributes must be atomic and single-valued; now part of the definition of a flat relation.
    2. 2NF (Codd, 1972): based on full functional dependency; no non-prime attribute depends on part of the primary key.
    3. 3NF (Codd, 1972): 2NF plus no transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on the primary key. 1NF and 2NF were proposed as stepping stones to 3NF. All three were first defined on the primary key, later generalized to all candidate keys.
    4. BCNF (Boyce and Codd, 1974): proposed as a simpler restatement of 3NF (every non-trivial FD has a superkey LHS) but turned out strictly stronger: it also forbids X→AX \rightarrow AX→A with XXX not a superkey and AAA prime.

    Later came 4NF (multivalued dependencies) and 5NF (join dependencies).

    Answer

    An unnormalized relation has non-atomic (multivalued, composite or nested) attribute values, i.e. is not in 1NF. Codd defined 1NF, 2NF (no partial dependencies) and 3NF (no transitive dependencies) in 1972 as successive steps; Boyce and Codd then defined the stricter BCNF (every determinant is a superkey).

    14.81NF, 2NF, 3NF on primary keys vs. generalE&N Ex. 14.8 · p. 497

    Define first, second, and third normal forms when only primary keys are considered. How do the general definitions of 2NF and 3NF, which consider all keys of a relation, differ from those that consider only primary keys?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Primary-key definitions

    • 1NF: every attribute value is atomic and single-valued (no multivalued/composite attributes, no nested relations).
    • 2NF: 1NF, and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (no non-prime attribute depends on a proper part of the PK). Example: EMP_PROJ is not 2NF since Ssn→Ename\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \textsf{Ename}Ssn→Ename with PK {Ssn,Pnumber}\{\textsf{Ssn},\textsf{Pnumber}\}{Ssn,Pnumber}.
    • 3NF: 2NF, and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key. Example: EMP_DEPT is not 3NF since Ssn→Dnumber→Dname\textsf{Ssn}\to \textsf{Dnumber}\to \textsf{Dname}Ssn→Dnumber→Dname.

    General definitions and the differences

    Primary-key versionGeneral version
    Keys consideredonly the chosen PKall candidate keys
    Prime attributeattribute of the PK (in effect)attribute of any candidate key
    2NFnon-prime attributes fully dependent on the PKno non-prime attribute partially dependent on any key
    3NF2NF and no non-prime attribute transitively dependent on the PKfor every non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A: XXX is a superkey or AAA is prime (implies 2NF; test directly)

    The general versions catch partial and transitive dependencies on secondary keys. In LOTS (keys Property_id# and {County_name, Lot#}), County_name→Tax_rate\textsf{County\_name} \rightarrow \textsf{Tax\_rate}County_name→Tax_rate is a partial dependency on the second key: LOTS passes PK-based 2NF (PK Property_id# is a single attribute) but fails general 2NF. Conversely, since “prime” now includes attributes of all keys, an FD whose RHS is part of another key no longer counts against 3NF.

    Answer

    PK-based: 1NF atomic values; 2NF no partial dependency on the PK; 3NF additionally no transitive dependency on the PK. The general definitions apply the same ideas to every candidate key and use “prime = in some candidate key”; general 3NF is the single test “every non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A has XXX a superkey or AAA prime”.

    14.9What 2NF avoidsE&N Ex. 14.9 · p. 497

    What undesirable dependencies are avoided when a relation is in 2NF?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Partial dependencies: a non-prime attribute functionally dependent on a proper subset of a candidate key. Such an attribute describes only part of the key, so its value is repeated for every tuple sharing that part. Example: in EMP_PROJ, Ssn→Ename\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \textsf{Ename}Ssn→Ename repeats Ename for each project of an employee and Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation}\textsf{Pnumber} \rightarrow \{\textsf{Pname},\textsf{Plocation}\}Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation} repeats project data for each worker (with the resulting anomalies). 2NF removes them by moving each such attribute into a relation with the key part it depends on: EP1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours), EP2(Ssn, Ename), EP3(Pnumber, Pname, Plocation).

    Answer

    Partial dependencies of non-prime attributes on part of a (candidate) key.

    14.10What 3NF avoidsE&N Ex. 14.10 · p. 497

    What undesirable dependencies are avoided when a relation is in 3NF?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on a key: key →Z→A\to Z\to A→Z→A where ZZZ is not a superkey (typically a non-prime attribute or set) and AAA is non-prime. Equivalently, a non-key attribute determining another non-key attribute. Example: EMP_DEPT with Ssn→Dnumber→{Dname,Dmgr_ssn}\textsf{Ssn}\to \textsf{Dnumber}\to\{\textsf{Dname},\textsf{Dmgr\_ssn}\}Ssn→Dnumber→{Dname,Dmgr_ssn} repeats department data per employee; 3NF splits it into ED1(Ename, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Dnumber) and ED2(Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn). Under the general definition, 3NF also excludes partial dependencies (it implies 2NF): it forbids every non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A with XXX not a superkey and AAA non-prime.

    Answer

    Transitive dependencies (non-prime attributes determined by non-key attributes), and, by the general definition, partial dependencies as well.

    14.11How the general definitions extend beyond primary keysE&N Ex. 14.11 · p. 497

    In what way do the generalized definitions of 2NF and 3NF extend the definitions beyond primary keys?

    Solution · written for this guide
    1. All candidate keys are used, not just the primary key: partial and transitive dependencies are tested against every key.
    2. Prime means belonging to any candidate key, so the set of attributes that are “protected” changes.
    3. General 2NF: no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any key.
    4. General 3NF: whenever a non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A holds, XXX is a superkey or AAA is prime. This one condition covers both partial and transitive dependencies, so 3NF can be tested directly without 2NF first.

    Example: LOTS(Property_id#, County_name, Lot#, Area, Price, Tax_rate) with second key {County_name, Lot#}. County_name→Tax_rate\textsf{County\_name} \rightarrow \textsf{Tax\_rate}County_name→Tax_rate is invisible to PK-based 2NF but is a partial dependency on {County_name, Lot#}; general 2NF catches it and splits off LOTS2(County_name, Tax_rate). Area→Price\textsf{Area} \rightarrow \textsf{Price}Area→Price then violates general 3NF (Area not a superkey, Price non-prime), giving LOTS1A and LOTS1B.

    Answer

    They replace “the primary key” by “every candidate key” (and prime by “in some candidate key”), and 3NF becomes a single test on all FDs: LHS a superkey or RHS prime.

    14.12BCNF vs. 3NFE&N Ex. 14.12 · p. 497

    Define Boyce-Codd normal form. How does it differ from 3NF? Why is it considered a stronger form of 3NF?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Definition

    RRR is in BCNF if whenever a non-trivial FD X→AX \rightarrow AX→A holds in RRR, XXX is a superkey of RRR.

    Difference

    3NF allows X→AX \rightarrow AX→A when XXX is a superkey or AAA is prime. BCNF drops the “or AAA is prime” clause. So a relation is in 3NF but not BCNF exactly when some X→AX \rightarrow AX→A holds with XXX not a superkey and AAA prime.

    Why stronger

    Every BCNF relation satisfies 3NF (clause (a) alone is enough), but not conversely. Example: TEACH(Student, Course, Instructor) with {Student,Course}→Instructor\{\textsf{Student},\textsf{Course}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Instructor}{Student,Course}→Instructor and Instructor→Course\textsf{Instructor} \rightarrow \textsf{Course}Instructor→Course. Keys: {Student, Course} and {Student, Instructor} (since {S,I}+=SIC\{S,I\}^+=SIC{S,I}+=SIC), so every attribute is prime. Instructor→Course\textsf{Instructor} \rightarrow \textsf{Course}Instructor→Course is allowed by 3NF (Course is prime) but violates BCNF (Instructor+^++ = {Instructor, Course}, not a superkey). The redundancy is real: “Mark teaches Database” repeats for each of Mark’s students. The lossless BCNF decomposition is TEACH1(Instructor, Course), TEACH2(Student, Instructor) (common attribute Instructor is a key of TEACH1), but it loses {Student,Course}→Instructor\{\textsf{Student},\textsf{Course}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Instructor}{Student,Course}→Instructor; 3NF can always be reached with dependency preservation, BCNF cannot.

    Answer

    BCNF: every non-trivial FD’s LHS is a superkey. It is 3NF without the exception for prime right-hand sides, so BCNF ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ 3NF but not conversely (TEACH is 3NF, not BCNF); it removes all FD-based redundancy, at the possible cost of losing a dependency.

    11  Chapter 14 problems

    Textbook exercises

    Conventions used in every solution below
    • The given FDs are the whole story. The FDs that hold are exactly those in F+F^+F+ (everything derivable from the given ones). Keys and normal forms are judged from F+F^+F+, never from sample data.
    • Attributes are atomic, so every schema is in 1NF unless the question says otherwise.
    • Left-hand sides are non-empty (an FD ∅→A\emptyset\to A∅→A would make AAA constant).
    • Closure algorithm. Start with X+:=XX^+ := XX+:=X; whenever an FD Y→ZY\to ZY→Z has Y⊆X+Y\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+, add ZZZ; stop when a full pass adds nothing. In the tables, “→Y→Z\xrightarrow{Y\to Z}Y→Z​” shows the order in which FDs fire.
    • Key-finding shortcut. An attribute on no right-hand side is in every key; an attribute on right-hand sides only (never on a left) is in no key. Search only the “middle” ones.
    • Splitting rule. If X→YX\to YX→Y violates the target NF in RiR_iRi​, replace RiR_iRi​ by X∪YX\cup YX∪Y and Ri−(Y−X)R_i-(Y-X)Ri​−(Y−X). The common attributes are XXX, a key of X∪YX\cup YX∪Y, so every such split is lossless.
    14.19University transcript database: FDs and 3NF/BCNF designE&N Ex. 14.19 · p. 497

    Suppose that we have the following requirements for a university database that is used to keep track of students’ transcripts:

    1. The university keeps track of each student’s name (Sname), student number (Snum), Social Security number (Ssn), current address (Sc_addr) and phone (Sc_phone), permanent address (Sp_addr) and phone (Sp_phone), birth date (Bdate), sex (Sex), class (Class) (‘freshman’, ‘sophomore’, …, ‘graduate’), major department (Major_code), minor department (Minor_code) (if any), and degree program (Prog) (‘b.a.’, ‘b.s.’, …, ‘ph.d.’). Both Ssn and student number have unique values for each student.
    2. Each department is described by a name (Dname), department code (Dcode), office number (Doffice), office phone (Dphone), and college (Dcollege). Both name and code have unique values for each department.
    3. Each course has a course name (Cname), description (Cdesc), course number (Cnum), number of semester hours (Credit), level (Level), and offering department (Cdept). The course number is unique for each course.
    4. Each section has an instructor (Iname), semester (Semester), year (Year), course (Sec_course), and section number (Sec_num). The section number distinguishes different sections of the same course that are taught during the same semester/year; its values are 1, 2, 3, …, up to the total number of sections taught during each semester.
    5. A grade record refers to a student (Ssn), a particular section, and a grade (Grade).

    Design a relational database schema for this database application. First show all the functional dependencies that should hold among the attributes. Then design relation schemas for the database that are each in 3NF or BCNF. Specify the key attributes of each relation. Note any unspecified requirements, and make appropriate assumptions to render the specification complete.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Each section has exactly one instructor, and Iname identifies the instructor. Why: the text says “each section has an instructor”; if team teaching were allowed, Iname would be multivalued and would need its own relation (SECTION_INSTR).
    2. A section is identified by (Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num). Why: Sec_num restarts at 1 for each course in each semester/year, so it is unique only within that combination.
    3. Major_code, Minor_code and Cdept hold department codes. Why: the names end in “code”; we take Cdept to be a code too, so all three are foreign keys to Dcode.
    4. A student has one grade per section taken. Why: “a grade record refers to a student, a particular section, and a grade”.
    5. No other FDs hold: e.g. Doffice does not determine Dphone, an address does not determine a phone, two departments may share an office building, two courses may share a name. Why: nothing in the requirements forces them; adding them would create extra 3NF violations.
    6. The current and permanent address/phone are single atomic values (no 1NF issue).

    Step 1: functional dependencies

    • FD1 Ssn →\to→ {Snum, Sname, Sc_addr, Sc_phone, Sp_addr, Sp_phone, Bdate, Sex, Class, Major_code, Minor_code, Prog}
    • FD2 Snum→Ssn\text{\textsf{Snum}} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Ssn}}Snum→Ssn   (so Snum also determines every student attribute)
    • FD3 Dcode→{Dname, Doffice, Dphone, Dcollege}\text{\textsf{Dcode}} \rightarrow \{\text{\textsf{Dname, Doffice, Dphone, Dcollege}}\}Dcode→{Dname, Doffice, Dphone, Dcollege}
    • FD4 Dname→Dcode\text{\textsf{Dname}} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Dcode}}Dname→Dcode   (both are unique)
    • FD5 Cnum→{Cname, Cdesc, Credit, Level, Cdept}\text{\textsf{Cnum}} \rightarrow \{\text{\textsf{Cname, Cdesc, Credit, Level, Cdept}}\}Cnum→{Cname, Cdesc, Credit, Level, Cdept}
    • FD6 {Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num}→Iname\{\text{\textsf{Sec\_course, Semester, Year, Sec\_num}}\} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Iname}}{Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num}→Iname
    • FD7 {Ssn, Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num}→Grade\{\text{\textsf{Ssn, Sec\_course, Semester, Year, Sec\_num}}\} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Grade}}{Ssn, Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num}→Grade

    Step 2: relations (one per group of FDs with the same determinant), keys, foreign keys

    • STUDENT(Ssn, Snum, Sname, Sc_addr, Sc_phone, Sp_addr, Sp_phone, Bdate, Sex, Class, Major_code, Minor_code, Prog)
      Candidate keys Ssn and Snum (Ssn+^++ = all by FD1; Snum+^++: FD2 gives Ssn, then FD1 gives all). Major_code → DEPARTMENT.Dcode, Minor_code → DEPARTMENT.Dcode (NULL allowed).
    • DEPARTMENT(Dcode, Dname, Doffice, Dphone, Dcollege); candidate keys Dcode, Dname.
    • COURSE(Cnum, Cname, Cdesc, Credit, Level, Cdept); key Cnum; Cdept → DEPARTMENT.Dcode.
    • SECTION(Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num, Iname); Sec_course → COURSE.Cnum.
    • GRADE_REPORT(Ssn, Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num, Grade); Ssn → STUDENT.Ssn; (Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num) → SECTION.

    Step 3: normal-form check

    In every relation the only non-trivial FDs that hold (projecting FD1–FD7) have a candidate key on the left: FD1, FD2 in STUDENT; FD3, FD4 in DEPARTMENT; FD5 in COURSE; FD6 in SECTION; FD7 in GRADE_REPORT. So every relation is in BCNF (hence 3NF). FD2 and FD4 relate two candidate keys; they do not violate BCNF because their left side is itself a key. The decomposition is dependency-preserving (each FD lives in one relation) and lossless (each relation is linked through a key / foreign key).

    Answer

    Five relations STUDENT, DEPARTMENT, COURSE, SECTION, GRADE_REPORT as above, all in BCNF, with keys {Ssn, Snum}, {Dcode, Dname}, Cnum, (Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num) and (Ssn, Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num).

    Valid alternatives. Many students have no minor, so Minor_code is often NULL; by Guideline 3 one may move it to STUDENT_MINOR(Ssn, Minor_code). A surrogate Section_id may replace the 4-attribute section key (then {Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num} stays a second candidate key, declared UNIQUE).

    What the grader checks

    Every FD written explicitly, including the “both unique” ones (Snum→Ssn\text{Snum} \rightarrow \text{Ssn}Snum→Ssn, Dname→Dcode\text{Dname} \rightarrow \text{Dcode}Dname→Dcode); the composite section key (Sec_num alone is not a key); every relation’s key stated and every FK named; a sentence justifying BCNF/3NF for each relation; unstated requirements (instructor per section, minor optional, Cdept as code) written as assumptions with reasons.
